newsitem.title: USA: AT&T, Bell merger unthinkable to experts - FCC.
newsitem.headline: AT&T, Bell merger unthinkable to experts - FCC.

text.p: A mega-merger of AT&T Corp. and regional phone company SBC Communications Inc. remains unthinkable in most antitrust experts' views, Federal Communications Commission chief Reed Hundt said Thursday.
"All of the published comments of the experts has been that it is unthinkable," Hundt said of the possible merger.

The FCC chairman said he was responding to the hypothetical merger after AT&T Chairman Robert Allen first raised the possibility in a speech on Tuesday and his company mailed the speech to hundreds of Washington decision-makers in an initial effort to sway opinion in favour of such a deal.

"I didn't see anything in (Allen's) argument that would suggest that any of these experts are about to change their views," Hundt said in an interview after speaking to 700 corporate executives at a Price Waterhouse conference here.
"If the FCC has to decide this issue and we go to those experts to decide whether to approve such a deal, you can predict what the overwhelming weight of opinion will be," Hundt told Reuters.

To date, neither AT&T or SBC have commented on whether they are holding talks to merge. Such a deal, if completed, would create a giant company with a stock market value of $110 billion, making it the largest corporate merger in history.

The Telecommunications Act of 1996 set forth a mechanism for doing away with legal barriers that have barred Baby Bells from entering the U.S. long-distance market since the break-up of the old AT&T telephone monopoly in 1984.
But many legal experts have argued that a merger between AT&T and the SBC, the former Southwestern Bell, would defeat efforts to forge greater competition in telecommunications.
In particular, they have said the combination of the AT&T and SBC would create an insurmountable barrier to competition in the Baby Bell's local phone service region.

AT&T is the nation's largest long-distance company, serving more than 80 million residential customers and 10 million businesses. SBC dominates local phone service in a seven-state area stretching from Texas to California.
Two weeks ago, Hundt announced he would resign as FCC chief once the Clinton administration finds a replacement.

During his appearance at the conference here on Thursday, Hundt was asked by interviewer Sir David Frost what government measures would be necessary to foster the goal of greater competition in the coming 10 years.

High on his list was a call for merger law reform. "We need to find a way to say 'No' to mergers instead of just sort of looking at them go by," he said. "There are some mergers coming up right now where we need to think about this," he said without mentioning specific companies.
